title: ISA Energy -- Brand Video Shoot Script
summary: Full shoot script for ISA Energy brand video. 5-min theater format. 3 acts, 9 beats, 4 subjects, b-roll location guide. Sedona Apr 3.
content:
ISA Energy -- Brand Video Script

Overview

  • Runtime: ~5 minutes (theater format)
  • Style: Cinematic narrative. Premium. Confident but not hype.
  • Delivery: Apr 17, 2026
  • Sedona interviews: Apr 3, 2026
  • Venue: Theater screening (plan for big screen, surround sound, dark room)

SHOT-BY-SHOT TIMELINE

This is the moment-to-moment visual flow. Every second accounted for. Read this and you should be able to see the video in your head.

ACT 1: THE PROBLEM (0:00 - 1:10)

Beat 1.1: The Invisible Dependency (0:00 - 0:30)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
0:00-0:02 BLACK. Text fades in: "ISA Energy" Silence. Low ambient hum begins. Theater -- let the room settle.
0:02-0:04 City skyline at dusk. Buildings lighting up one by one. Wide, locked tripod. Hum builds. Tempe Town Lake or stock.
0:04-0:06 Phone charging on nightstand. Close-up, handheld, shallow DOF. Narration begins: "Everything runs on electricity." Intimate, personal scale.
0:06-0:08 Hospital monitors. Green waveforms. Beeping. Macro lens. "Every light, every screen..." Stakes -- lives depend on this.
0:08-0:10 Data center rack. LEDs blinking. Handheld tracking shot. "...every system keeping someone alive right now." Industrial scale.
0:10-0:12 Slow push on a light switch. Someone's hand flips it. Light fills room. "And almost nobody thinks about where it comes from." The simplest gesture.
0:12-0:14 Brief black or dark transition. Beat. Silence. Let the line land.
0:14-0:28 HUNTER talking head. Medium close-up, lab background soft. Hunter answers: "When did you first realize how fragile the thing we all depend on actually is?" This is the first face we see. It matters. Warm key light, slight off-center. He should feel real.
0:28-0:30 B-roll: Power line silhouette against sky. Hunter's last words trail as we transition. Visual bridge to 1.2.

Beat 1.2: The Century-Old Grid (0:30 - 0:55)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
0:30-0:34 Wide drone shot: transmission lines crossing desert. Slow lateral move. Narration: "The grid that powers it all was built more than a century ago." US-60 or stock. Scale that dwarfs people.
0:34-0:37 Massive electrical substation. Locked wide. Heat shimmer if possible. "Centralized generation. Massive infrastructure." APS substation from road. Telephoto.
0:37-0:40 Cooling towers of a power plant. Steam rising. "Long-distance transmission with energy lost at every step." Stock footage. Heavy, industrial feel.
0:40-0:42 Workers inspecting aging infrastructure. Hard hats, clipboards. Narration fades. Stock or pickup day.
0:42-0:53 SKYLAR talking head. Clean workspace background. Skylar answers: "When you talk to potential customers and partners, what do they say about the current state of energy infrastructure?" Skylar grounds it in real conversations. Market-facing energy.
0:53-0:55 B-roll: Single power line stretching to horizon. Transition beat. Visual punctuation.

Beat 1.3: The Gap Renewables Can't Close (0:55 - 1:10)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
0:55-0:58 Wind turbines at sunset. Blades slowing. Golden light. Narration: "Renewables are part of the answer." Stock or Painted Rock Dam area.
0:58-1:01 Solar panels. Clouds passing, shadow falling across them. Timelapse. "But the sun goes down. The wind stops." Loop 202 solar farms or stock.
1:01-1:05 Single house in remote desert. Wide. Isolated. No power lines visible. "And the places that need power most are often the farthest from any grid." Hwy 87 toward Payson. Telephoto.
1:05-1:08 Slow zoom on the dark windows of the remote house. No lights inside. Music shifts. Tone changes from problem to possibility. This is the turn. Act 2 is coming.
1:08-1:10 Brief black. Beat. Breathe before the breakthrough.

ACT 2: THE BREAKTHROUGH (1:10 - 3:55)

Lab Team Footage woven throughout. Between every interview segment, we cut to candid team shots. The audience should feel like they're inside the lab.

Beat 2.1: The Origin (1:10 - 1:50)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
1:10-1:14 Sedona lab exterior. Wide establishing shot. Red rocks in background. Slow push toward entrance. Narration: "Nearly a decade ago, a team in Sedona..." Shoot day. Golden light if afternoon.
1:14-1:17 Door opens. We step inside. Handheld, following someone in. "...started asking a different question:" First time inside. Discovery moment.
1:17-1:20 Lab interior reveal. Equipment on benches. Whiteboards. Warm, real. Not corporate. "What if you didn't need the grid at all?" Slow pan. Let the audience take it in.
1:20-1:23 Lab candid: Two team members at whiteboard, sketching. Marker squeaking. Ambient lab sounds. Natural, not staged.
1:23-1:25 Close-up: lab notebook pages with handwritten equations. Quiet. Texture. Real work.
1:25-1:42 HUNTER talking head. Lab behind him, slightly out of focus. Equipment visible. Hunter answers: "Take me back to the beginning. What was the original insight?" This is the origin story. Give him room. 15-17 seconds of clean answer.
1:42-1:45 Lab candid: Someone carrying a prototype component across the lab. Hunter's words trail. Bridge to tech explanation.
1:45-1:50 Lab candid: Harrison at his workstation. Shot from behind/side. We see him AND the equipment. Deep focus. Soft transition music. Sets up Harrison before we hear from him.

Beat 2.2: What the Technology Actually Does (1:50 - 2:35) CRITICAL BEAT

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
1:50-1:53 Extreme close-up: ISA coil device. Rack focus from coil to oscilloscope behind it. Narration: "ISA's technology captures ambient energy..." Macro lens. Precision.
1:53-1:56 Oscilloscope waveform. Clean sine wave. Screen fills frame. "...energy that already exists in the environment..." The science made visual.
1:56-1:59 Harrison's hands adjusting the transformer coil. Deliberate, careful movements. "...and converts it into usable power." His hands tell the story of craft.
1:59-2:02 The moment: device powers a light bulb. It turns on. Hold the shot. "Directly at the point of consumption." THIS is the money shot. Let it breathe.
2:02-2:04 Signal generator and amplifier running. LEDs active. "No grid connection. No fuel source. No dependence on weather." Technical credibility.
2:04-2:30 HARRISON talking head. Lab background. Equipment visible but soft. Harrison answers: "In the simplest terms you can, explain what this system actually does." THE most important soundbite. 25+ seconds. If he nails a clean explanation, DO NOT CUT. Let it run. Medium close-up. He should feel authoritative but human.
2:30-2:33 Lab candid: Harrison and team member calibrating coil together. Two people, one problem. Harrison's last words. Shows teamwork, not solo genius.
2:33-2:35 Close-up: oscilloscope reading. Numbers on screen. Data. Quiet beat. Visual proof before we talk about proof.

Beat 2.3: The Proof (2:35 - 3:10)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
2:35-2:38 Scientist observing measurements. Over-the-shoulder shot looking at equipment. Narration: "And they proved it." Simple. Direct.
2:38-2:41 Validation study documents. Close-up. Official letterhead. Graphs. "Independent validation confirmed net energy gain." Paper proof. Tangible.
2:41-2:44 Oscilloscope showing net energy gain reading. Push in slow. "Not on paper. In the lab." Data on screen. No hype.
2:44-2:47 Lab notebook pages. Handwritten data entries. Pencil marks. "Measured, documented, and repeatable." Human touch on scientific process.
2:47-3:05 HARRISON talking head. Same setup. Harrison answers: "What did the validation study actually show? Walk me through the moment you saw the results." 18 seconds. The proof delivered with understatement.
3:05-3:08 Lab candid: Team gathered around monitor, watching results. Someone nods. Ambient. Authentic reaction shot.
3:08-3:10 Lab candid: Equipment rack power-up. LEDs sequence on. Fans spin. Mechanical sounds. Energy. Forward motion.

Beat 2.4: Why Now (3:10 - 3:55)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
3:10-3:13 Dense city at night. Every building lit. Aerial or high angle. Narration: "The timing matters." Phoenix downtown or stock.
3:13-3:16 Construction cranes. New buildings going up. "Global energy demand is accelerating faster than infrastructure can grow." Rio Salado area, Tempe.
3:16-3:19 EV charging station. Car plugged in. Lights blinking. "AI. Electric vehicles." Any Tesla Supercharger.
3:19-3:22 Server farm exterior. Massive building. Industrial cooling units. "Entire economies going digital." CyrusOne or QTS, Price Rd. From parking lot.
3:22-3:25 Quick montage: phone screen, laptop, smart home device, medical scanner. "The grid was never built for this." 1-second cuts. Demand is everywhere.
3:25-3:45 SKYLAR talking head. Same clean setup. Skylar answers: "Why does this technology matter right now? What's changed in the market?" 20 seconds. Market urgency. He should feel energized.
3:45-3:50 Lab candid: Close-up hands soldering connections. Sparks. Precision. Skylar's words trail. The team is building while the market waits.
3:50-3:55 Wide shot: lab from above (if possible) or wide interior. Team at work. Activity. Music swells slightly. The lab is alive. Transition to Act 3.

ACT 3: THE FUTURE (3:55 - 5:00)

Beat 3.1: What This Means for the World (3:55 - 4:35)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
3:55-3:58 Modern home at night. Warm light from windows. Inviting. Narration: "Imagine a home that powers itself." Arcadia neighborhood. Drive-by exterior.
3:58-4:01 Office building. Fully powered. Night. Every floor lit. "A business that never worries about the grid going down." Scottsdale or Tempe office park.
4:01-4:04 Remote community. Small structures. Then -- lights come on. "A community that was never connected to the grid in the first place..." Stock or composite. The contrast matters.
4:04-4:07 Close-up: child's face lit by a lamp turning on. Wonder. "...finally with reliable power." Stock. Emotional beat.
4:07-4:10 Electric vehicle charging. Night. Clean energy flowing. Brief pause in narration. Visual punctuation.
4:10-4:30 HUNTER talking head. Lab background. Warm. Hunter answers: "When this technology is fully deployed, what does the world look like?" 20 seconds. Grounded vision. Not "we'll change the world." Specific.
4:30-4:35 Wide landscape: Sedona at late afternoon. Red rocks. Space. Hunter's last words. Setting up the emotional close.

Beat 3.2: The Close (4:35 - 4:55)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
4:35-4:38 ISA team walking together outside the lab. Golden hour. Casual. Narration: "The future of energy is not bigger plants and longer power lines." Natural, not posed. End-of-day energy.
4:38-4:41 Golden hour light through lab windows. Dust particles in the beam. Interior. "It's smaller, closer..." Beautiful light. Cinematic.
4:41-4:43 Final device shot. The coil. Still. Powerful in its simplicity. "...and already here." The technology. Quiet confidence.
4:43-4:53 HUNTER talking head. Tightest framing yet. Just his face and shoulders. Hunter answers: "What drives you to keep going? What is this really about for you?" The emotional close. 10 seconds of truth. This is the last human voice we hear.
4:53-4:55 Wide shot: Sedona landscape at dusk. Red rocks, open sky. Hold. Hunter's last word echoes. Then silence. Music only. Earned moment.

Beat 3.3: End Card (4:55 - 5:00)

Time What's on screen Audio Notes
4:55-4:57 Black. ISA Energy logo fades in. Clean. Centered. Music resolves to final note. Simple. Premium.
4:57-4:59 Tagline appears below logo. Silence. Let it sit.
4:59-5:00 URL or contact info fades in below. Hold. Silence. Theater -- the screen stays up.

DETAILED BEAT DESCRIPTIONS (Reference)

Beat 1.1: The Invisible Dependency

The point: The audience should feel how deeply electricity runs through every moment of modern life -- so deeply that most people never think about it. Visual: Quick montage. City skyline at dusk lighting up. Phone charging on a nightstand. Hospital monitors running. Data center racks blinking. All handheld, intimate, slightly desaturated. Each shot holds for 1-2 seconds. Narration/text overlay: "Everything runs on electricity. Every light, every screen, every system keeping someone alive right now. And almost nobody thinks about where it comes from." Interview question: "Hunter -- when did you first realize how fragile the thing we all depend on actually is?" (Hunter answers) Fallback: If Hunter's answer doesn't land cleanly, narration carries the full beat. His soundbite becomes supplemental texture laid over b-roll rather than driving the point.

Beat 1.2: The Century-Old Grid

The point: The system powering the modern world was designed over 100 years ago. It is centralized, inefficient, and showing its age. Visual: Wide drone shot of transmission lines crossing desert. Massive electrical substation. Cooling towers of a power plant. Workers inspecting aging infrastructure. These shots should feel heavy and industrial -- scale that dwarfs people. Narration/text overlay: "The grid that powers it all was built more than a century ago. Centralized generation. Massive infrastructure. Long-distance transmission with energy lost at every step." Interview question: "Skylar -- when you talk to potential customers and partners, what do they say about the current state of energy infrastructure?" (Skylar answers) Fallback: Narration bridges alone. Skylar's answer is ideal here because it grounds the problem in real conversations with real people, not theory. If the soundbite runs long, trim to a single punchy sentence and let narration do the rest.

Beat 1.3: The Gap Renewables Can't Close

The point: Solar and wind are helping but they are not always-on. The world needs something that works anytime, anywhere. Visual: Wind turbines at sunset, slowing. Solar panels losing light as clouds pass. A single house in a remote location, far from any power line. The isolation should feel real. Narration/text overlay: "Renewables are part of the answer. But the sun goes down. The wind stops. And the places that need power most are often the farthest from any grid." Interview question: None for this beat. Narration carries it. This is a fast transition beat that sets up Act 2. Fallback: N/A -- narration-only beat.

ACT 2: THE BREAKTHROUGH (~150-180 sec)

NEW: Lab Team Footage Block -- Weave throughout Act 2. Candid shots of the ISA team doing real work in the Sedona lab. This is the heartbeat of the act. The audience should feel like they are inside the lab watching a team build something that matters.

Lab team shots to capture:

  • Harrison and team member calibrating the transformer coil assembly
  • Close-up hands: soldering connections, adjusting oscilloscope probes, writing in lab notebooks
  • Two team members at a whiteboard sketching circuit diagrams, debating an approach
  • Someone carrying a prototype component across the lab
  • Equipment rack power-up sequence (LEDs lighting, fans spinning, screens flickering to life)
  • Team gathered around a monitor watching test results come in (authentic, not staged)
  • Harrison at his workstation deep in focus, shot from behind/side so we see him AND the equipment

How to shoot low-cost: All lab team footage shoots during the Apr 3 Sedona day. No extra location. No extra crew. Capture these candid moments BETWEEN interviews while subjects warm up or reset. Dedicate the 11:30am-12:30pm lab b-roll block specifically to team candids. Have team members doing actual work (not posing). Direct them to ignore the camera.

Beat 2.1: The Origin

The point: Introduce ISA and the idea that started it all. A small team in Sedona asked a question nobody else was asking. Visual: Cut to Sedona lab exterior. Slow push toward the entrance. Then inside: the lab, warm and real. Equipment on benches. Whiteboards covered in notes. This is not a gleaming corporate R&D center. This is where real work gets done. Narration/text overlay: "Nearly a decade ago, a team in Sedona started asking a different question: what if you didn't need the grid at all?" Interview question: "Hunter -- take me back to the beginning. What was the original insight that made you believe this was possible?" (Hunter answers) Fallback: If Hunter tells the story too long or too abstract, use the best 8-10 seconds and let narration frame the rest: "ISA Industries was founded on a single idea -- that energy already exists in the environment around us. The question was whether you could capture it."

Beat 2.2: What the Technology Actually Does

The point: Explain the technology in plain language. Ambient energy capture -- converting energy that already exists in the environment into usable electrical power, directly where it is needed. No grid. No fuel. No intermittency. Visual: Close-up of the ISA coil device. Oscilloscope waveform readings. Harrison adjusting the transformer coil. Device powering a light bulb. Signal generator and amplifier running. These shots should feel precise and real -- not flashy, not staged. Narration/text overlay: "ISA's technology captures ambient energy -- energy that already exists in the environment -- and converts it into usable power. Directly at the point of consumption. No grid connection. No fuel source. No dependence on weather." Interview question: "Harrison -- in the simplest terms you can, explain what this system actually does and why it's different from anything else out there." (Harrison answers) Fallback: Harrison is the technical voice. If his answer goes too deep, use the plainest 10-12 seconds and bridge with narration. The audience needs to understand the concept, not the physics. If he nails a clean explanation, let it breathe -- this is the most important soundbite in the video.

Beat 2.3: The Proof

The point: This is not theoretical. It has been tested. Independently validated. The results are real. Visual: Scientist observing equipment measurements. Validation study documentation. Close-up of oscilloscope power readings showing net energy gain. Lab notebook pages. Clean, steady shots. No hype. Data on screen. Narration/text overlay: "And they proved it. Independent validation confirmed net energy gain. Not on paper. In the lab. Measured, documented, and repeatable." Interview question: "Harrison -- what did the validation study actually show? Walk me through the moment you saw the results." (Harrison answers) Fallback: If Harrison's answer is too technical, narration carries the proof beat: "An independent systems engineer spent weeks testing ISA's claims. The conclusion: net energy gain. The system produces more power than it consumes." Harrison's reaction shot or a brief clip of him describing the moment overlays the narration.

Beat 2.4: Why Now

The point: The timing is not accidental. Energy demand is surging (AI, EVs, global electrification). The existing grid cannot keep up. ISA's technology arrives at exactly the moment the world needs it most. Visual: Dense city at night, every building lit up. Construction cranes. EV charging stations. Server farms. The visual message: demand is accelerating. Narration/text overlay: "The timing matters. Global energy demand is accelerating faster than infrastructure can grow. AI. Electric vehicles. Entire economies going digital. The grid was never built for this." Interview question: "Skylar -- why does this technology matter right now, specifically? What's changed in the market that makes ISA's timing so critical?" (Skylar answers) Fallback: Skylar's strength is market context. If the answer doesn't connect timing to urgency clearly enough, narration bridges: "The market for decentralized energy is not coming. It's here. And ISA is the only company with a working system that captures ambient energy at the point of use."

ACT 3: THE FUTURE (~60-75 sec)

Beat 3.1: What This Means for the World

The point: Paint the picture. Homes that generate their own power. Businesses free from grid dependency. Remote communities with reliable electricity for the first time. This is not incremental improvement. This is a fundamental shift. Visual: Modern home lighting up at night (warm, inviting). Office building fully powered. Factory machinery running. Remote village with lights on. Electric vehicle charging. Each shot should feel aspirational but grounded -- real places, real people, real power. Narration/text overlay: "Imagine a home that powers itself. A business that never worries about the grid going down. A community that was never connected to the grid in the first place -- finally with reliable power." Interview question: "Hunter -- when this technology is fully deployed, what does the world look like? What changes for ordinary people?" (Hunter answers) Fallback: If Hunter goes too big-picture or too abstract, trim to the strongest sentence and let the visual montage carry the emotion. Narration can supplement: "ISA's vision is not just a better energy company. It's a world where power is generated where it's used, by the people who need it."

Beat 3.2: The Close

The point: Confidence without arrogance. ISA is not promising to save the world. They are building something that works. And they are just getting started. Visual: ISA team walking through the lab together. Golden hour light through the Sedona lab windows. Final wide shot of the Sedona landscape at dusk. The team is small but focused. The energy is forward motion. Narration/text overlay: "The future of energy is not bigger plants and longer power lines. It's smaller, closer, and already here." Interview question: "Hunter -- what drives you to keep going? What is this really about for you?" (Hunter answers -- this is the emotional close) Fallback: If Hunter's answer does not land as a natural closer, use his best line from any point in the interview as the final soundbite. The last words the audience hears should feel earned and honest. Worst case, end on narration: "ISA Industries. Energy, everywhere." over the Sedona dusk wide shot.

Beat 3.3: End Card

The point: Brand moment. Clean. Memorable. Visual: Black or deep dark frame. ISA Energy logo fades in. Tagline below. Hold for 3 seconds. URL or contact info fades in below. Narration/text overlay: "ISA Industries" (logo) / tagline / website Interview question: None. Fallback: N/A.

INTERVIEW GUIDE

Hunter (CEO/Founder)

Role in story: The visionary. The person who saw a problem nobody else was solving and decided to spend a decade of his life on it. Hunter gives the audience permission to believe this is real -- not because he hypes it, but because he speaks with the quiet conviction of someone who has been in the lab doing the work.

Questions:

  1. "When did you first realize how fragile the energy system we all depend on actually is?" -- serves Beat 1.1 -- hoping for: a personal, specific moment. Not a statistic. A realization that hit him and stuck.
  2. "Take me back to the beginning. What was the original insight that made you believe ambient energy capture was possible?" -- serves Beat 2.1 -- hoping for: the origin story in human terms. What he saw or experienced that made him say "this could work."
  3. "When this technology is fully deployed, what does the world look like? What changes for ordinary people?" -- serves Beat 3.1 -- hoping for: a grounded, specific picture of the future. Not "we will change the world." More like "a family in rural Arizona will never lose power again."
  4. "What drives you to keep going? What is this really about for you?" -- serves Beat 3.2 -- hoping for: the emotional truth. Why this matters to him personally. This is the potential closer for the entire video.
  5. "What is the single biggest misconception people have about energy and where it comes from?" -- serves Beat 1.1 or 1.2 (flex) -- hoping for: a sharp, quotable line that reframes how the audience thinks about the grid.
  6. "Describe what it felt like the first time the system actually worked." -- serves Beat 2.3 (flex) -- hoping for: an authentic emotional beat. The moment of proof. This could be the most powerful 5 seconds in the video if he's honest about it.

Skylar (Sales/Business Dev)

Role in story: The translator. Skylar connects the technology to the real world -- market need, customer pain, commercial timing. Where Hunter speaks to the "why" and Harrison speaks to the "how," Skylar speaks to the "who cares and why now."

Questions:

  1. "When you talk to potential customers and partners, what do they say about the current state of energy infrastructure? What problems come up over and over?" -- serves Beat 1.2 -- hoping for: specific, real-world pain points. Not abstract market analysis. Actual things people say in meetings.
  2. "Why does this technology matter right now, specifically? What has changed in the market that makes ISA's timing so critical?" -- serves Beat 2.4 -- hoping for: urgency and specificity. AI demand, grid strain, electrification trends. A clear case that the window is now.
  3. "What is the commercial case for ambient energy capture? Who are the first customers and what does it solve for them?" -- serves Beat 2.4 (flex) -- hoping for: concrete use cases. Not "everyone." Specific sectors, specific problems, specific value.
  4. "What do people not understand about how far along ISA actually is?" -- serves Beat 2.3 (flex) -- hoping for: a moment of credibility. ISA is not a whiteboard company. They have a working system. Skylar can bridge between the tech proof and the market opportunity.
  5. "If everything goes according to plan over the next 12-18 months, what does ISA look like?" -- serves Beat 3.1 (flex) -- hoping for: forward motion without overpromising. Manufacturing, deployment, partnerships. The transition from lab to market.

Harrison (Asst Lead Science)

Role in story: The engineer. The person who understands the technology at the deepest level and can make it accessible. Harrison brings credibility through competence -- not charisma, not vision, but the quiet authority of someone who builds things that work.

Questions:

  1. "In the simplest terms you can, explain what this system actually does and why it is different from anything else out there." -- serves Beat 2.2 -- hoping for: the plainest, clearest explanation of the technology possible. If he can say it in 15 seconds and a non-engineer understands it, that is the gold standard soundbite.
  2. "What did the validation study actually show? Walk me through the moment you saw the results." -- serves Beat 2.3 -- hoping for: proof delivered with understatement. The data showed net energy gain. Let the weight of that land without overselling it.
  3. "What makes this system reproducible? How do you know it was not a one-time result?" -- serves Beat 2.3 (supporting) -- hoping for: scientific credibility. Repeatability is the difference between a demo and a breakthrough.
  4. "What is the hardest technical challenge you have solved so far, and what told you the approach was working?" -- serves Beat 2.2 (flex) -- hoping for: a specific engineering moment that reveals the depth of the work. Not jargon. A problem and how they solved it.
  5. "What would you say to a skeptical engineer who hears 'ambient energy capture' and assumes it is too good to be true?" -- serves Beat 2.2 or 2.3 (flex) -- hoping for: a direct, confident, data-backed response. Not defensive. Just "here is what we measured."

Jared (Business/Background)

Role in story: The operator. Jared is not a primary voice in this video. He is background muscle -- funding, scale, operations. Only pull him in if there is a specific point about business scale, manufacturing readiness, or capital strategy that Hunter and Skylar cannot cover.

Questions:

  1. "Where does ISA stand right now in terms of the business infrastructure needed to scale this technology?" -- serves Beat 2.4 or 3.1 (flex) -- hoping for: a grounded answer about manufacturing, supply chain, or capital readiness. The "we are not just a lab" beat.
  2. "What does the funding landscape look like for a company like ISA right now?" -- serves Beat 2.4 (flex) -- hoping for: context on why the capital environment is favorable. Only use if Skylar does not cover this.
  3. "What is the biggest operational challenge between where ISA is today and full-scale deployment?" -- serves Beat 3.1 (flex) -- hoping for: honesty about what is hard. This adds credibility if used sparingly.

Usage note: Jared is the safety net. If Hunter, Skylar, and Harrison deliver strong interviews, Jared may not appear in the final cut. That is fine. Shoot his interview anyway. Having it gives options in the edit.

SHOOT DAY CHECKLIST

What to Bring

  • Cinema camera package (primary + backup body)
  • Interview lens: 50mm or 85mm (shallow depth of field for interview intimacy)
  • B-roll lenses: 24mm wide, 100mm macro (for device close-ups and oscilloscope screens)
  • Tripod + fluid head for interviews
  • Handheld rig or gimbal for lab b-roll and walkthroughs
  • 2x LED panel lights (key + fill for interviews)
  • 1x LED tube or edge light (hair/rim light, separation from background)
  • Shotgun mic on camera for b-roll ambient sound
  • 2x lavalier mics (wired or wireless) for interviews
  • Boom mic + operator if crew allows
  • Audio recorder (backup to camera audio)
  • 4+ memory cards (shoot heavy, do not run out)
  • Batteries for everything, plus chargers
  • Gaffer tape, clamps, extension cords
  • Laptop for on-set review
  • Release forms for all interview subjects
  • Shot list printout (this document)
  • Drone (if permitted for Sedona exteriors -- check local regs)

Interview Setup Notes

  • Backdrop preference: Lab environment for Hunter and Harrison. The equipment, whiteboards, and workbenches should be visible but not distracting. Slightly out of focus behind them. This is not a boardroom company.
  • Skylar: Office or clean workspace setting. Whiteboard or screen behind him if possible. He represents the market-facing side.
  • Jared: Same setup as Skylar. Keep it simple.
  • Framing: Medium close-up. Eyes in upper third. Slight off-center. Subject looks just off-camera (interviewer sits next to the lens, not behind it).
  • Lighting: Warm key light, soft fill. Minimal shadows. The Sedona lab has natural light -- use it as a starting point and supplement. Avoid sterile/corporate lighting.
  • Background depth: Keep at least 6-8 feet between subject and background for good separation and bokeh.
  • Audio: Lav mic on every interview subject. Boom as backup. Room tone recording before first interview (30 seconds of silence in each setup location).

Order of Interviews (Who First and Why)

  1. Harrison (first) -- Harrison is the most technical and likely the least camera-comfortable. Get him early when he is fresh and before he watches others, which could make him self-conscious. His explanation of the technology (Beat 2.2) is the most critical soundbite in the video.
  2. Hunter (second) -- Hunter is the founder and will likely be the most natural on camera. He has the most questions and covers the widest range (origin, vision, emotion). Give him time but keep him focused. His answers drive Act 1 and Act 3.
  3. Skylar (third) -- Skylar covers market and timing. His energy should be up after watching the technical team go. His questions are more conversational and market-facing.
  4. Jared (last) -- Jared is the safety net. Shoot him last. If time runs short, he is the one to cut. If the first three interviews are strong, Jared's interview is insurance for the edit.

Time Estimate Per Person

  • Harrison: 20-30 minutes (allow extra time for re-takes if technical explanations need simplifying)
  • Hunter: 30-40 minutes (most questions, widest range, give him room to tell stories)
  • Skylar: 20-25 minutes (focused questions, conversational pace)
  • Jared: 15-20 minutes (lean interview, only if time allows)
  • B-roll: 60-90 minutes minimum (lab walkthrough, device close-ups, team candids, Sedona exteriors, golden hour shots)
  • Setup/teardown: 30-45 minutes on each end
  • Total shoot day: 4-6 hours on location

Golden Hour Note

If the shoot runs into late afternoon, prioritize Sedona exterior b-roll during golden hour (roughly 5:30-6:30pm in early April). The landscape shots for the closing beat (3.2) will be significantly more cinematic in that light. Plan the b-roll block accordingly -- do not burn golden hour on interviews.

THEATER FORMAT NOTES

At 5 minutes on a big screen:

  • Every shot needs to hold up at high resolution. Shoot 4K minimum, deliver in 4K.
  • Slow camera movement reads better than fast cuts in a theater. Let shots breathe.
  • Sound design matters more. Ambient lab sounds, subtle music swells, silence between beats.
  • The extra runtime vs. the 2-3 min version comes from: (1) letting interview answers run longer, (2) lab team candids woven throughout Act 2, (3) b-roll establishing shots that breathe instead of flash-cutting.
  • Color grade should be consistent across all locations. The Sedona warmth is the anchor. Phoenix shots grade to match.
